newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine inflation rises, economists not alarmed.
newsitem.headline: Philippine inflation rises, economists not alarmed.

text.p: The Philippine inflation rate grew slightly to 5.1 percent in December, but the figure was within government projections and economists said they did not expect a radical shift in monetary policy to temper its rise.

The National Statistics Office on Monday announced a 5.1 percent inflation rate in December, up from 4.5 percent in November. The December rate was slightly higher than the 4.9 percent projected by analysts in a recent Reuters poll.
The annual average inflation for 1996 grew to 8.4 percent from 8.1 percent the previous year, the statistics agency said.
The numbers were well within the government's projection of less than 6.5 percent in December and an annual average of between 7.5 and 8.5 percent.
"The point here is price stability," Bong Bongolan, economist at PrimeEast Securities, said.
The consumer price index inched up by only 0.8 percent based on month-on-month change.
The statistics office attributed the rising inflation to higher petroleum prices and electricity rates, especially in the provinces.
Prices for all commodity groups, including the food, beverage and tobacco index, registered higher rates in December, except for miscellaneous items, which were unchanged at 1.7 percent.

"The 5.1 percent inflation is pretty respectable considering that the economy is growing ... It says a lot for the way the economy is being run," said Johnny Noe Ravalo, chief economist of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.
Philippine inflation had been hovering at double-digit levels in the last part of 1995 and early part of 1996 due to poor harvests.

For the first time since 1987, growth is seen outpacing inflation. Inflation is expected to slow this year to between six to seven percent on an annual average basis, while gross national product is seen growing by seven to eight percent.

Al Rillo, economist at DBS Securities, said the inflation situation should not warrant any radical tightening of the money supply, which had been lower as of November than was required by the liquidity growth programme set by the International Monetary Fund.
In fact, Rillo sees a gradual easing of interest rates due to the differential between Philippine and U.S. interest rates.
He said monetary officials would like to keep the peso stable by discouraging the influx of arbitrage money.
The Central Bank had cut the reserve requirements imposed on banks' deposits starting on Monday, freeing some 6.7 billion pesos ($254 million) into the system.
He said higher liquidity should not push up inflation because the additional funds could be easily absorbed by the growing economy.
"The economy has enough productive capacity to absorb the increase in liquidity," Rillo said.
PrimeEast's Bongolan said the situation provided a perfect opportunity to adopt a more aggressive stand on the overvalued peso.
"It's a good time to jump-start the economy. We need a bolder exchange rate policy to address the issue of widening trade gap and demands of the exporters," he added.
Analysts said rising petroleum prices also would have a minimal impact on the prices of commodities, which have been stabilised by good harvests.
